speaker: Chris Urmson
title: The Road to Autonomy: Chris Urmson on Building Aurora
question: In autonomous trucking, why does conventional pulsed LiDAR hit a physical limit at highway speeds?
guest: The way conventional LiDAR works is you shoot laser beams out into the world and time how long they go out and come back. The speed of light is constant, so you can figure out distance from that. The farther you shoot out, the more the beam gets dispersed and the less energy comes back. So if you want to see farther, you need to shoot more energy out. At some point, you're shooting out so much energy that, depending on the wavelength, you'll either burn people's retinas or boil the aqueous fluid in their eyeballs, which you don't want to do. Meanwhile, the kinetic energy for a truck driving at 70 miles an hour versus a car in an urban environment at 15 to 25 is about 50-fold, so the stopping distance is much larger. We knew conventional LiDAR's limit wasn't far enough to drive trucks safely at highway speeds. That's why we moved to frequency-modulated continuous wave LiDAR: instead of looking for a bright returning spike, it measures wave interference and phase differences—a self-heterodyne effect that gives a 10- to 20-fold signal amplification, letting you see much farther with the same eye-safe energy.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Conventional pulsed (time-of-flight) LiDAR runs into a range problem that is set by physics and eye-safety rules, not engineering polish.

A fully loaded truck at highway speed needs roughly 200–300+ metres to detect a hazard, decide, and stop. Pulsed LiDAR measures distance by timing reflected laser pulses, and the returned signal falls off steeply with distance (roughly with the square of range for extended targets), so a small, dark object such as a tyre fragment or a pedestrian in dark clothing returns only a handful of photons at those ranges. The obvious fix is more laser power, but most pulsed systems operate at 905 nm, where the eye focuses light onto the retina, so eye-safety limits cap pulse energy. Direct detection also cannot distinguish its own photons from sunlight or other LiDARs, so the weak return gets lost in noise.

There are secondary limits too: each pulse must return before the next is unambiguously sent, capping point density at long range, and velocity must be inferred across multiple frames, costing reaction time.

This is why trucking developers such as Aurora pursue FMCW LiDAR at 1550 nm, which uses coherent detection and measures velocity instantly.

models.answer: At highway speeds, fully loaded Class 8 trucks need hundreds of meters to stop, requiring reliable detection of small, dark hazards like tire debris at 300 meters or beyond. Conventional pulsed time-of-flight LiDAR—typically using 905-nanometer lasers—hits a fundamental physical ceiling at these ranges due to signal attenuation, eye-safety caps, and speed-of-light timing limits. Return light intensity falls with the square of distance, and up to the fourth power for objects smaller than the laser beam, so distant, low-reflectivity targets reflect only a few photons that are easily overwhelmed by ambient sunlight and receiver noise. Sensors cannot simply emit brighter pulses to compensate: because the human eye focuses 905-nanometer light onto the retina, Class 1 eye-safety regulations strictly cap peak pulse energy. Simultaneously, avoiding range ambiguity requires waiting for each pulse’s round-trip echo before firing again, throttling pulse rates at long distances and forcing a trade-off between range, point density, and frame rate—while still needing multiple sequential frames to infer an obstacle’s velocity.

noweb.answer: At highway speeds, a fully loaded autonomous truck needs over 150 meters to stop, requiring reliable detection of low-reflectivity hazards like dark vehicles or tire debris 250 to 300 meters ahead. Conventional pulsed time-of-flight LiDAR—typically operating near 905 nanometers—hits several coupled physical limits at that range. Because 905-nanometer light focuses onto the human retina, eye-safety regulations strictly cap transmitted pulse energy. Meanwhile, return signal strength plummets with the inverse square of distance—and up to the inverse fourth power for small, unresolved road debris—until the few returning photons are drowned out by ambient sunlight and detector noise in direct-detection receivers. Compounding this photon-budget bottleneck, the finite speed of light requires waiting longer for distant echoes before firing the next pulse to avoid range ambiguity, directly trading maximum range against angular resolution and frame rate. Finally, pulsed LiDAR measures only position rather than instantaneous Doppler velocity, forcing software to infer motion across multiple frames and adding critical reaction latency at high closing speeds.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Conventional pulsed LiDAR hits a physical limit at highway speeds because it can't see dark objects far enough ahead to give a heavy truck time to stop.

**The required range.** A loaded truck at about 65 mph needs roughly 150–200 m to stop safely. Add time for the system to perceive the hazard and react, and it needs to detect small, dark (about 10% reflective) objects like tire debris or a stalled car at 250–400 m.

**Why pulsed LiDAR falls short.** It fires short laser bursts and times their echoes. The returning signal weakens with roughly the square of distance, so far-away, low-reflectivity targets send back very few photons. Eye-safety rules cap laser power, especially at the common 905 nm wavelength, and sunlight and other LiDARs add noise. Together these limit reliable detection to about 150–200 m.

**A built-in trade-off.** Each pulse has to come back before the next one fires, or distances get confused. Reaching 300 m takes about 2 µs per pulse round trip, which caps how many points per second the sensor can collect.

**No direct speed reading.** Pulsed LiDAR measures position only. Speed has to be estimated by comparing several frames, which adds delay.

That's why truck developers like Aurora and Aeva use FMCW LiDAR. It measures speed directly through the Doppler effect and reaches 400 m or more at 1550 nm.
